title: Life in Christ: The Gift of Eternal Life

paragraphs.text: Before you begin
Moses Afolabi • Illustrated study edition • 2026

Read the whole Bible passage before working through a chapter. Scripture quotations use the King James Version. Modern application scenes and illustrations are teaching examples. They do not describe documented events or verified personal testimonies.
Historical accounts are identified and accompanied by source links. Consider their particular setting as you reflect on the biblical passage.

Take time to read the explanation, study the visual summary, and complete the practice in your own notebook. Discuss difficult questions with a trusted pastor or mature believer. Return to the chapter after trying its suggested action.
The PDF contains still illustrations. The separate animated companion adds gentle motion and chapter prompts.
Contents

2. The Son Who Came Near 10
3. Peace Through the Cross 16
4. The Risen Lord and a New Beginning 22
5. Faith and the Ground of Assurance 28

Chapter 1 The Life God Gives
Receive the gift through Christ. Reading the whole passage can expose an assumption that acceptance must first be earned.
Read John 3:1–21, John 17:1–5, and Romans 6:23.
Begin with the giver
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. — John 3:16, KJV

The first action in this sentence belongs to God. He loves and gives. The person who believes responds to the Son whom God has given. Read the verse slowly enough to distinguish the giver, the gift, the response, and the promised life. A reader worried about having an impressive spiritual history can begin with what God has done. The invitation concerns faith in His Son. Our need is real, and the gift comes from His love.

The surrounding passage takes sin seriously. Jesus speaks about judgment and about people loving darkness. God's love does not require Him to pretend that our choices have been harmless. It brings the Son into the very world that needs rescue. When explaining the gospel to another person, hold together the seriousness of human wrongdoing and the generosity of
God's provision. Neither needs to be exaggerated to make the other meaningful.
What everlasting life means
And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent. — John 17:3, KJV

Jesus describes eternal life through knowing the Father and the Son. This is personal knowledge grounded in who God reveals Himself to be. It includes trust, relationship, and a life shaped by that relationship. Everlasting life extends beyond death, and it also reaches the believer's present. A person can begin to pray, listen to Scripture, receive forgiveness, and learn obedience now. These practices express the relationship the gift has opened.

Knowing someone takes attention. When reading a Gospel, ask what the passage reveals about Jesus before asking how to improve your routine. Notice whom He welcomes, what He confronts, and how He speaks about His Father. Write one observation in a complete sentence. Then turn it into a response. If He shows compassion to a person others overlook, ask where you need to give someone patient attention today.
Biblical encounter · Nicodemus brings his question

Nicodemus comes to Jesus by night in John 3. He has religious knowledge and recognizes that Jesus' works point to God's presence. Jesus nevertheless speaks to him about being born again. Nicodemus struggles to understand, and Jesus continues the conversation. The account gives an educated, respected person room to acknowledge what he cannot yet explain.

Read verses 3–8 without trying to reduce the Spirit's work to a technique. New birth comes from God. A particular emotional atmosphere, impressive vocabulary, or repeated formula cannot manufacture it. Nicodemus needs to hear what Jesus says about the Son. Your own questions may differ, but you can bring them honestly to Scripture and to a trustworthy Christian who will read the passage with you.
A practical conversation about receiving

Imagine a fictional engineer in Toronto who has begun attending church. She assumes she must repair every weakness before she can approach Christ. Her friend opens John 3 and asks her to identify the action God has already taken. Then they read Romans 6:23 together. The contrast between wages and gift helps her name the assumption she brought into the conversation.
For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. — Romans 6:23, KJV

A gift can be received with gratitude and then change how the recipient lives. Read the whole of Romans 6 to see why grace leads into a new relationship to sin. The engineer can trust Christ and also take responsibility for a dishonest report she previously submitted. Making that correction follows the direction of her new life. It cannot buy the life God gives.
Visual summary
God gives His Son
Faith receives the Savior
Eternal life reaches daily living
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Reflection and response

Write four short statements beginning with God gives, Jesus reveals, I need, and I will respond. Keep each statement tied to a verse in this chapter. Read your statements with a mature believer and ask where your explanation is unclear. If you want to trust Christ, speak to Him honestly about your sin and your reliance on Him. You can pray in ordinary words. Ask a local church to help you learn the faith, discuss baptism, and grow in fellowship.
Prayer. Father, thank You for giving Your Son. Help me understand the life You offer and receive Your grace with faith. Teach me to know You through Jesus Christ. Amen.
Chapter 2 The Son Who Came Near
A patient conversation gives real questions room to be heard. Let the Gospel reveal who Jesus is before deciding what He must be like.
Read John 1:1–18, Colossians 1:15–20, and Hebrews 2:14–18.
Read the opening claim carefully
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. — John 1:1, KJV

John begins before the public ministry, before Bethlehem, and before creation. The Word already was. He distinguishes the Word's relationship with God while also affirming His divine identity. Read verses 1–3 together. Creation comes into being through Him. The Gospel asks us to understand Jesus in the light of this opening, then shows His words and actions in particular human encounters.

This matters when someone treats Jesus only as an inspiring adviser. His teaching has authority because of who He is. The reader is invited to trust the One through whom all things were made. We should therefore resist reshaping Him into a spokesman for whichever ambition we already hold. Read an entire encounter and let His actual words question your expectations.
The Word became flesh
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth. — John 1:14, KJV

The Son's coming involves genuine human life. The Gospel records hunger, weariness, friendship, grief, and bodily suffering. His humanity makes these encounters more than a performance. Hebrews 2 connects His sharing our humanity with His merciful priestly ministry. He is able to help those who are tempted. We can therefore bring weakness to Him without assuming He is indifferent to human experience.

Grace and truth appear together in John's description. We need both when approaching a difficult part of our lives. Truth allows us to admit what happened. Grace gives us reason to approach the Savior with that admission. A person who has disappointed a family can name the failure plainly and seek His mercy. A person who feels unseen can bring that loneliness into prayer and ask for wise human companionship.
Biblical encounter · Jesus speaks to the Samaritan woman

Read John 4:4–30, 39–42. Jesus speaks with a woman at a well and addresses her actual situation. The conversation moves through water, worship, and His identity. She has questions, and He answers with particular attention to what she says. The account ends with other people coming to hear Him. They eventually speak of knowing Him through hearing for themselves.

Observe the patience of the conversation. Jesus neither flatters her nor reduces her to the most painful part of her history. When sharing your faith, learn this attention to the person. Ask what they understand, answer the question they actually asked, and leave room for them to read the Gospel. You do not have to invent certainty about their motives or force every conversation into the same script.
Reconciliation has a center
And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, I say, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven. — Colossians 1:20, KJV

Read Colossians 1:15–23 to see the scope and the center of Paul's teaching. The Son's supremacy and the cross belong in one account. We cannot explain reconciliation merely as learning to feel better about ourselves. Alienation, sin, and peace with God are involved. The cross gives Christian hope its particular shape and directs our attention toward Christ's action.

Consider a fictional graduate student in Singapore who wants to know whether Christian faith requires switching off difficult questions. A patient mentor opens John 1 and invites her to follow the Gospel's claims. They distinguish questions about the text from assumptions about religious people. The mentor does not claim to answer everything in one evening. They agree to read John 4 next and write down what the encounter reveals about Jesus.
Visual summary
The Word is God
The Word became flesh
Grace and truth come near
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Study that leads to worship

Make two columns in your notebook. In the first, record what John 1 says about the Word's identity. In the second, record what it says about His coming among us. Add one observation from Hebrews 2 about His help. Then explain in your own words why His identity and His humanity both matter. Pray about one weakness you have kept distant from Him, and arrange a conversation if you need support from another believer.
Prayer. Lord Jesus, help me receive the witness of Scripture about who You are. Thank You for coming among us in grace and truth. Teach me to trust Your mercy and listen to Your words. Amen.
Chapter 3 Peace Through the Cross
Grace gives courage to correct a dishonest account. Name the omission and restore the proper credit.
Read Romans 3:21–26, Romans 5:1–11, and Luke 23:32–43.
Let the passage explain the need
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: — Romans 3:23–24, KJV

Paul describes a need shared by humanity and a provision located in Christ. Sin includes particular deeds and the deeper condition from which they arise. We should resist reducing it to unfortunate feelings or measuring it only by comparison with someone worse. The passage gives us a truthful place to stand before God. We need His grace, and He provides redemption through Jesus Christ.

To be justified concerns God's righteous verdict. It is received freely by grace through Christ's redemption. The word freely challenges the habit of treating religious effort as payment for acquittal. The word redemption directs attention to the cost borne by the Redeemer. The gift is free to the person receiving it because of Christ's costly work. Read verse 25 and note how Paul connects faith with Christ's blood.
Peace rests on what Christ has done
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: — Romans 5:1, KJV

The therefore carries the argument forward. Peace with God follows justification by faith. It is more substantial than having a calm afternoon. A believer may feel anxious about a consequence while relying on Christ for peace with God. Learning this distinction allows prayer to remain honest about emotion. You can say that you feel unsettled and still give thanks for the access described in Romans 5:2.

Read Romans 5:6–8. God's love is displayed in Christ's death for people who need rescue. We do not establish that love by creating a sufficiently impressive record after conversion. The cross reveals its character. This can change how you confess. You can name a real sin directly, ask for forgiveness, and seek the help needed to turn from it. Hiding the event behind vague language only makes practical repair more difficult.
Biblical encounter · A criminal appeals to Jesus
And he said unto Jesus, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise. — Luke 23:42–43, KJV

Read the preceding conversation. One criminal acknowledges the justice of his own sentence and the innocence of Jesus. Then he appeals to Him. Jesus answers with a promise of being with Him. The encounter gives powerful testimony to the sufficiency of Christ's mercy. The criminal has no opportunity to construct a new reputation before making his appeal.

His circumstances also require careful application. We should not use the account to dismiss baptism, discipleship, restitution, or the responsibilities of people who continue living. The promise demonstrates the Savior's authority to receive a person who trusts Him. Those given further days can use them to learn obedience. Mercy opens that future and gives it direction.
A worked example of confession and repair

Imagine a fictional supervisor in Manchester who concealed a colleague's contribution to gain recognition. After reading Romans 3, he stops comparing his conduct with more dramatic wrongdoing. He names his own deed. In prayer he asks for forgiveness on the ground of Christ's grace. He then prepares a factual correction to the manager who received the inaccurate account.

The correction might say, “The analysis I presented included Priya's research, which I failed to acknowledge. Please correct the record.” He should avoid adding details that transfer blame or demand immediate reassurance from his colleague. There may still be consequences. Receiving mercy does not give him authority to dictate how quickly others must trust him. Grace gives him courage to do the truthful work before him.
Visual summary
Christ provides redemption
Faith receives peace with God
Grace leads into truthful repair
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Examine the ground of your confidence

Write the difference between a consequence you must address and a verdict you are trying to purchase. Read Romans 5:1 aloud and identify the person through whom peace comes. Then name one action that follows from gratitude for that peace. If the harm is complicated, seek wise help before contacting someone in a way that could cause further injury. Keep the goal of truth and responsible repair clear.
Prayer. Father, thank You for the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Help me confess plainly, trust Your grace, and take responsibility for the correction that belongs to me. Amen.
Chapter 4 The Risen Lord and a New Beginning
New life reaches the next response. A practical pause can help a person use words truthfully and with self-control.
Read Luke 24:1–35, 1 Corinthians 15:1–8, and Romans 6:1–14.
The gospel includes resurrection

For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures: — 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, KJV

Paul identifies events at the center of the message he received and passed on. Jesus died for our sins, was buried, and rose again. The passage continues with witnesses to the risen Christ. Christian faith concerns what God has done in history, and the resurrection is integral to its good news. Treat it with the same seriousness as the cross when explaining why we trust Jesus.

Read the rest of 1 Corinthians 15 over several sittings. Paul argues that the resurrection has consequences for preaching, faith, forgiveness, and future hope. A vague sense that goodness will eventually win cannot carry the argument. His claim is specific. Christ has been raised. The believer's hope of bodily resurrection rests on the risen Lord.
Biblical encounter · The road to Emmaus

In Luke 24, two disciples travel with sorrow and confused expectations. Jesus joins them, asks about their conversation, and opens the Scriptures concerning Himself. They later recognize Him and return to tell the others. Notice how their understanding changes through the encounter. They bring disappointment into a conversation that is answered through Scripture and the presence of the risen Jesus.

A disappointed believer may need time to name the expectation that has collapsed. Ask what you expected Christ to do and where that expectation came from. Then read what the passage actually says. The disciples' experience gives room for honest grief while directing attention toward God's larger purpose. We can seek that understanding without claiming that every personal disappointment has an explanation already available to us.
Count yourself alive to God
Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord. — Romans 6:11, KJV

Read Romans 6:1–14 as a connected argument. Paul speaks of union with Christ in His death and resurrection, then directs the believer to reckon accordingly. Reckoning involves taking God's declaration seriously when understanding your position and choosing your conduct. It reaches the ordinary use of your body, attention, and abilities. Verse 13 asks believers to yield themselves to God and their members as instruments of righteousness.

The practical question becomes specific. How will you use your speech in the next conversation? What will you do with the record you could alter? Which arrangement makes obedience easier to practice? You can change access to a recurring temptation, ask for accountability, and choose a faithful action. These are ways of yielding your life to God in the light of the life you have received.
Practice a new response before the old situation returns

Consider a fictional designer in Seoul who routinely responds to criticism by posting angry messages. He reads Romans 6 and identifies his phone, his words, and his desire to protect his status as concrete places for response. He decides to save drafts privately, wait until he has read the feedback carefully, and ask one clarifying question before answering publicly.

This arrangement will not remove every angry feeling. It gives him a responsible way to act while learning. After the next difficult exchange, he reviews what he actually wrote and whether he represented the other person fairly. He brings any failure into confession and revises the arrangement. A new beginning can grow through such deliberate acts of faithfulness.
Visual summary
Christ died and rose again
Believers share life in Him
Yield your conduct to God
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
A resurrection-shaped review

Write three statements from 1 Corinthians 15:3–4 without changing their meaning. Then read Romans 6:11–13 and identify one part of your daily conduct that needs to reflect new life. Plan the response in advance, including the time and support it will require. At the end of the week, describe what changed in your conduct. Keep the report factual, and give thanks for grace while continuing to learn.
Prayer. Risen Lord, thank You for the life You give. Help me understand my union with You and yield my words, habits, and abilities to Your purposes today. Amen.
Chapter 5 Faith and the Ground of Assurance
Place the promise beside the feeling. Assurance grows through attention to the testimony concerning Christ.
Read John 6:35–40, 1 John 5:9–13, and Hebrews 10:19–23.
Listen to God's testimony
And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life. — 1 John 5:11–12, KJV

John directs the reader to God's testimony concerning His Son. Eternal life is located in Him. The following verse explains John's purpose in writing to those who believe on the name of the Son of God. He wants them to know that they have eternal life. The written witness supplies a place to return when emotions fluctuate or memories of failure become loud.

Assurance should therefore grow through attention to the One being trusted and the promise being received. Ask what the passage says about Christ before asking whether your feelings are sufficiently strong. Faith can be expressed simply and honestly. “Lord Jesus, I am relying on You” identifies its object. Repeating words mechanically cannot replace that trust, and an intense experience cannot replace the content of the gospel.
Receive the invitation to come
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. — John 6:37, KJV

Read John 6:35–40. Jesus connects coming to Him with believing in Him and speaks of the Father's will. Pay attention to the breadth of His welcome. A person troubled by an embarrassing history can bring that history into His presence. The invitation gives grounds to seek Him honestly. It also helps a church welcome people patiently as they learn to live in the faith.

Suppose a fictional new believer in Vancouver repeatedly measures her salvation by how enthusiastic she felt during worship. A mentor asks her to read the same passage on a quiet Tuesday. They identify the promise, the speaker, and the person invited to come. She writes these facts beside her emotional description. This allows both to be acknowledged while placing the grounds of confidence in Christ's word.
Historical testimony · Charles Wesley reads and seeks

Charles Wesley's journal for May 1738 describes conversations, prayer, and sustained reading of Scripture while he sought faith and assurance. In the entry for May 17, he records reading Luther on Galatians and reflecting on justification by faith. His account of May 21 records a change in his confidence in Christ. Read this as his personal testimony, with its particular language and setting. It illustrates a search directed toward the gospel. It cannot establish a required emotional sequence for everyone else. Charles Wesley's journal, May–August 1738
Bring examination into the light

First John also calls believers to walk in the light, acknowledge sin, and love one another. Read 1 John 1:5–2:2 alongside 5:11–13. The letter gives both a promise and a truthful way to face wrongdoing. If you discover a serious inconsistency in your conduct, bring it to God and seek help in turning from it. Avoid using assurance language to excuse what the same letter confronts.

Some readers find themselves checking their feelings and motives without reaching a conclusion. A trusted pastor can help them read a whole passage instead of isolating one anxious phrase. Persistent distress may also call for qualified support. Seeking such help is compatible with prayer. The aim is to understand and respond faithfully, rather than manufacture a feeling under pressure.
Visual summary
Read God’s testimony
Trust the Son it reveals
Walk honestly in His light
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Build a clear account of your trust

Answer four questions in your notebook. Who is Jesus? What has He done? What does He promise those who come to Him? On what am I relying? Use the passages in this chapter to revise vague answers. Share them with a mature believer who can ask useful questions. Then choose one expression of gratitude or obedience for the coming week. Let your response grow from the promise you have read.
Prayer. Father, help me hear Your testimony about Your Son. Establish my confidence in Jesus Christ and teach me to walk honestly in His light. Amen.
Chapter 6 Remaining in Christ in Ordinary Life
Build a realistic rhythm of attention to Scripture within the week you actually have.
Read John 15:1–17, Luke 10:38–42, and Galatians 5:16–26.
Follow the picture Jesus gives
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing. — John 15:5, KJV

A branch receives its life through its connection to the vine. Jesus uses this relationship to explain dependence and fruitfulness. Read verses 1–8 and notice the Father's care, the words of Jesus, and the call to remain. The picture directs attention toward continuing relationship. A branch cannot produce life by admiring another branch or by describing how fruitful it hopes to become.

In practice, abiding includes receiving Christ's words, bringing requests to Him, and responding to His commands. The chapter connects these with love. Verse 12 makes the command concrete by directing disciples toward love for one another. When reviewing a spiritual routine, ask how it helps you receive His words and love the people you actually meet. A crowded schedule of religious activities can still require careful examination.
Biblical encounter · Martha and Mary

Read Luke 10:38–42 without inventing motives the text does not state. Martha receives Jesus and becomes distracted by much serving. Mary sits at His feet and hears His word. Martha brings her complaint to Jesus, and He addresses her anxiety and distraction. The account gives a busy disciple permission to examine the condition of attention within useful work.

A caregiver cannot always leave a responsibility unfinished. The question can still be practical. Which tasks are necessary today? Which have grown through fear of disappointing someone? Where is a small opportunity to listen to Scripture attentively? A brief passage read with care can give a person something to carry into the next task. Ask for help with an unrealistic workload where that is possible.
Recognize fruit by its character
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. — Galatians 5:22–23, KJV

Read these verses within Paul's call to walk in the Spirit. The qualities concern character and relationships. They are more searching than public success alone. You can complete an important task while speaking harshly to the people helping you. You can also display patience during a week when visible results are modest. Use the passage to examine the manner of your conduct as well as its output.

Choose one quality and define what it would look like in a particular relationship. Patience might involve allowing an older relative time to explain a need. Self-control might involve closing an argument instead of sending another accusatory message. Gentleness might involve correcting a volunteer privately with specific facts. Such acts make the language of fruit observable without pretending you can measure a person's whole spiritual life from one incident.
A worked rhythm for a demanding week

Imagine a fictional restaurant manager in Madrid who works changing shifts. She chooses a repeatable sequence rather than a fixed hour that often fails. After breakfast, whenever it occurs, she reads a short Gospel passage. Before opening work messages, she asks which part of that passage needs attention in her conduct. During a break, she returns to one sentence. In the evening she records one opportunity to practice it.

The rhythm can be revised when family needs or work hours change. Its value lies in helping her attend and respond. If she misses a day, she resumes at the next available point. She also remains connected to a congregation that can encourage her, correct her understanding, and share practical burdens. Abiding has a personal dimension and a community setting.
Visual summary
Receive Christ’s words
Pray and respond in love
Review the fruit in relationships
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Shape your own practice

Write the next seven days as they are likely to happen, including travel, care, and work. Identify a realistic cue for reading and prayer. Choose a passage short enough to consider carefully. Ask one question about Christ and one about the response He invites. At the end of the week, assess whether the arrangement helped you listen and act. Keep what served that purpose and adjust what repeatedly failed.
Prayer. Lord Jesus, teach me to remain in You through the ordinary demands of life. Let Your words shape my attention and let the Spirit's fruit be visible in my relationships. Amen.
Chapter 7 Sharing Life in the Household of Faith
Belonging involves both service and truthful conversation. Clear responsibilities help willing people contribute sustainably.
Read Acts 2:41–47, 1 Corinthians 12:12–27, and Ephesians 4:1–16.
New life brings us among people
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers. — Acts 2:42, KJV

Luke describes people who receive the message and enter a shared pattern of learning, fellowship, meals, and prayer. Read the passage as an account of the early believers before applying it to a modern congregation. Their shared life includes attention to actual needs. Belonging becomes visible through time, resources, and care. The gospel gathers people whose growth will involve one another.

A new believer may need help understanding the ordinary practices of a church. Someone can explain where Bible study takes place, whom to ask about baptism, and how to seek prayer. A welcome is more useful when it includes an understandable next step. Do not assume that a person unfamiliar with church vocabulary understands what a leader means by fellowship or discipleship.
Each member has a place and a responsibility
Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular. — 1 Corinthians 12:27, KJV

Read Paul's body illustration from verse 12. Different members contribute differently, and none can dismiss another as unnecessary. The image challenges both pride and withdrawal. A person with a visible role needs the gifts of people whose contribution is quieter. A person who feels unimportant can consider the actual service they are equipped to offer. Belonging gives room to learn what a sustainable contribution might be.

Ask about a real need before volunteering for a title. If someone needs transport, clarify times and the return journey. If a ministry needs help with accounts, confirm the skills and oversight involved. If a person needs counseling, recognize when listening should lead to a qualified referral. Christian willingness benefits from clear responsibilities, appropriate preparation, and accountability.
Historical testimony · Bunyan is encouraged to serve

In his own account of being called to ministry, John Bunyan describes believers who recognized a gift and repeatedly encouraged him to speak. He first did so privately and with hesitation. Their response and continued encouragement contributed to his later public ministry. This is a particular historical account, rather than a pattern every vocation must repeat. It illustrates how a Christian community can help someone test a contribution through actual service and feedback. John Bunyan, Grace Abounding, account of his call to ministry, sections 265–268
Learn to speak truth in a relationship
But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ: — Ephesians 4:15, KJV
Truth and love govern the manner of growth. A disagreement about a roster can become an opportunity to practice both.

State what happened, ask what you have missed, and explain the effect on the work. Avoid attaching a verdict about the person's motives to an event you have not discussed. Equally, avoid hiding a repeated problem behind politeness that leaves someone else carrying its cost.

Imagine a fictional volunteer in Nairobi who has been assigned three weekends without being consulted. She asks for a private conversation and brings the schedule. She explains which commitment she can keep and which must be reassigned. The coordinator acknowledges the oversight and changes the process for future rosters. The example shows a practical form of truth in love. A different response may require another responsible leader to help.
Visual summary
Learn within the household
Offer and receive appropriate help
Speak truth in love
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Take a next step in belonging

Write the name of a congregation where you can learn Scripture and participate responsibly. If you are already involved, identify one relationship in which you need either to receive help or offer it. Ask a specific question this week. Agree what the next step involves and when it will be reviewed. Keep your commitment proportionate to your actual capacity, and tell people promptly if circumstances change.
Prayer. Father, thank You for receiving us into the household of faith. Help me learn, serve, receive correction, and care for others with truth and love. Amen.
Chapter 8 Hope Strong Enough to Face Death
Hope and sorrow can be present together. Practical care and a patient presence give comfort a visible form.
Read John 11:17–44, 1 Corinthians 15:20–28, 50–58, and 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18.
Let Jesus speak into grief
Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: — John 11:25, KJV

Martha speaks with Jesus after her brother's death. Her words include both grief over His absence and confidence in what God can do. Jesus directs her attention to Himself as resurrection and life. Read the whole conversation. The promise has a person at its center. Christian hope rests on Him and on His victory over death.

The same chapter records that Jesus wept. His tears allow sorrow and hope to be seen together. We need not make grieving people prove their faith by appearing cheerful. A friend may need someone to sit quietly, prepare a meal, or listen to the same memory more than once. Ask what would help today and fulfill the small commitment you make. Leave room for the person's grief to have its own pace.
Distinguish the sign and the final hope

Jesus calls Lazarus from the tomb in John 11. The event is a sign that reveals His authority. Paul in 1 Corinthians 15 speaks of the final resurrection and transformed life in the victory of Christ. Read the passages together with attention to their distinct purposes. We should not use Lazarus' restoration as a promise that every bereavement will be reversed immediately in the same way.
But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept. — 1 Corinthians 15:20, KJV

Firstfruits connects Christ's resurrection with the harvest that follows. Paul grounds the future of those who belong to Christ in what has happened to Him. This gives hope a foundation larger than the strength of our imagination. We can confess that future even while acknowledging questions about what we cannot presently see.
Comfort one another with care
Wherefore comfort one another with these words. — 1 Thessalonians 4:18, KJV

Read verses 13–18 before using the closing instruction. Paul addresses grief and the hope of the Lord's coming. Comfort involves bringing the promise into a relationship with someone who needs it. Timing and tone matter. Ask whether the person would welcome reading the passage together. Listen after reading. You do not have to answer every question about suffering to remain faithfully present.

Consider a fictional family in São Paulo after a grandmother's death. One member offers to manage practical calls, another brings food, and another reads the passage with relatives who request prayer. They avoid claiming to know why she died. They remember her honestly and speak of the hope of resurrection in Christ. Their different contributions allow comfort to reach both the immediate burden and the deeper sorrow.
Hope gives work its horizon

Paul concludes 1 Corinthians 15 by calling believers to steadfastness and abundant labor in the Lord. The resurrection gives present faithfulness a future horizon. A kind act, a truthful witness, and patient service can matter even when their result is not immediately visible. Read verse 58 after the entire argument. Its encouragement rests on the victory Paul has described.

Ask where grief, disappointment, or weariness has made a faithful task feel pointless. Choose a manageable responsibility and seek appropriate help to carry it. Hope does not require you to accept every demand. It can help you give yourself to the particular work that is yours while allowing others to share the burden.
Visual summary
Christ is risen
His people await resurrection
Hope supports comfort and service
